assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks at the 10^-18 level are a precision-measurement achievement of the first rank: the magic-wavelength idea turns many atoms into a clock whose uncertainty is set by the atom and not by the trap. They open tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and a redefinition of the second. From my own field's viewpoint this is atomic structure and light-shift theory made into an instrument, with very clear fundamental content.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and demonstrated the first lattice clocks; Jun Ye pushed stability and systematic control to the 10^-18 regime and the many-body clock. Two names give a clean, defensible configuration. Other groups (e.g. NIST ion and Sr clock work, PTB) are important but not required for a fair prize.
assessment.maturity: Very mature: many independent laboratories worldwide reproduce 10^-18-level performance and compare clocks over fibre and free space. The interpretation is stable and recognition would be timely, as the redefinition of the second is under discussion.
uncertainties: Whether a prize should be shared with the ion-clock lineage (Wineland recognised 2012) or with frequency-comb contributors already honoured in 2005 is a question for the committee.
I rely on my own recollection of the history, not on verified documents.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The recollision model explains the unexpected high-harmonic plateau with a simple image: tunnel out, accelerate in the laser field, return and recombine. It is the conceptual basis of attosecond science and of strong-field physics generally, and it has been confirmed in great quantitative detail. It is clearly original and lastingly important.
assessment.attribution: Corkum's semiclassical three-step model (1993) and Schafer et al. (1993) were near-simultaneous; Lewenstein et al. (1994) supplied the quantum-mechanical strong-field-approximation derivation. Credit is genuinely shared and a three-person configuration is plausible, though Krause, Kulander and others are also in the story. I note my close collaboration with the 2023 laureate and my field proximity, which I would disclose in deliberation.
assessment.maturity: Very mature, with abundant independent experimental confirmation, from high-harmonic spectra to orbital tomography and attosecond measurements. Timing is delicate because the 2023 prize already honoured attosecond pulse generation, so a second prize in the same area needs a distinct justification.
uncertainties: Possible overlap with the 2023 prize in the committee's judgement.
Allocation among Corkum, Schafer, Lewenstein and other contributors such as Kulander and Krause is unresolved.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Trapping, cooling and precisely measuring antihydrogen and antiprotons tests CPT and the matter-antimatter asymmetry directly. Spectroscopy of antihydrogen (1S-2S, hyperfine, gravity response) is genuinely fundamental and technically very demanding, in the spirit of precision atomic physics.
assessment.attribution: Gabrielse (ATRAP, single-particle antiproton and positron methods, antihydrogen production) and Hangst (ALPHA, antihydrogen trapping and spectroscopy) are the main figures. The ATHENA/AEgIS/ASACUSA/ALPHA collaborations make it a collective effort and the credit structure is not fully clean.
assessment.maturity: Fairly mature for the trapping and first spectroscopy results, but precision so far is far below that of hydrogen, so the strongest tests of CPT are still ahead. Recognition may be somewhat early.
uncertainties: Precision of antihydrogen tests is not yet competitive with matter hydrogen.
Credit among ATHENA, ATRAP and ALPHA personnel (including Rolf Landua, Jeffrey Hangst, Gabrielse, and others) is not fully captured by the supplied names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realised Hubbard-model physics, the superfluid to Mott insulator transition and quantum simulation in a controllable setting. The work gives new understanding of strongly correlated quantum matter and links atomic physics to condensed matter. Its importance is high and the fundamental motivation is clear.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller (with Jaksch) proposed the Bose-Hubbard realisation and the simulation programme; Greiner, Bloch and Hänsch (Munich) and Esslinger (Zürich) did the key experiments. The group is large; Jaksch is not in the supplied names. A theory plus experiment combination (Zoller/Cirac and Bloch) is plausible but arguably leaves out Greiner and Esslinger.
assessment.maturity: Mature: many laboratories use quantum gas microscopes and lattice simulators, and results are cross-checked against theory. Overlaps conceptually with the 1997 and 2001 laser-cooling and BEC prizes and with the 2025 quantum-technology theme.
uncertainties: Selecting three from five credited names leaves a disputed allocation.
The prominence of experimental versus theoretical credit is unresolved.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The observation of the Higgs boson completes the Standard Model's electroweak sector and confirms a mechanism recognised in 2013. As an experiment it is a major accomplishment of detector physics, data analysis and organisation, and its importance is beyond doubt. I defer to colleagues in particle physics on the finer points.
assessment.attribution: The discovery was made by two collaborations of thousands; individual credit is difficult. Gianotti (ATLAS spokesperson at the time of discovery) and Della Negra and Virdee (CMS pioneers, CMS spokesperson) are plausible representatives, but the Nobel statutes' limit of three people and the collective nature are a serious obstacle, as is the role of Jenni and Evans.
assessment.maturity: Mature, as results have been confirmed by both experiments, and properties are being measured. A prize for the discovery itself would be late in some sense since the 2013 prize recognised theory.
uncertainties: Attribution to a few named individuals for a collaboration of thousands is contentious.
Choice among Gianotti, Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee is uncertain.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry uses matter-wave coherence for precision measurement of gravity, rotation and fundamental constants, and for tests of the equivalence principle. It is a direct demonstration of quantum mechanics at a macroscopic scale and a precision tool of lasting value.
assessment.attribution: Pritchard (first atom interferometers with material gratings and light), Bordé (Ramsey-Bordé interferometer theory and early measurement) and Kasevich (light-pulse interferometry, gravimetry) are central. Chu (already a laureate), Mlynek, Keith, Ketterle and others contributed as well, so the allocation is not obvious.
assessment.maturity: Mature in technique, with commercial and metrological applications, but the large fundamental tests (e.g. gravitational-wave detection, dark-matter searches) are not yet decisive.
uncertainties: Overlap with earlier laureates such as Chu and the laser-cooling prize.
Which contributions are decisive is not clear to me.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Squeezed vacuum injection beats the standard quantum limit in interferometric measurement, and is now used routinely in gravitational-wave detectors. It joins quantum optics theory with a practical sensitivity gain, and is a clear case of a quantum-mechanical idea changing a large instrument.
assessment.attribution: Caves proposed squeezed-state interferometry (1981); Kimble and Slusher produced early squeezed light experiments; Schnabel and Mavalvala developed implementation in the detectors. The credit is distributed across theory, early optical experiments and implementation, and the supplied three-person subset is a judgement.
assessment.maturity: Established in operating detectors (GEO600, LIGO, Virgo), so the confirmation is strong, but it is an enabling technique within an observatory that was already recognised in 2017.
uncertainties: Whether it constitutes a stand-alone discovery or an improvement of an already honoured detector.
Attribution among Caves, Kimble, Slusher, Walls, Schnabel, Mavalvala is uncertain.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum key distribution links quantum foundations (Bell's theorem, no-cloning) with information security and has led to real-world networks. The conceptual originality of BB84 and the entanglement-based E91 protocol is clear.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard (BB84) and Ekert (E91) are the natural trio. The list includes two spellings of Ekert's name, so I use the single form 'Artur Ekert' and treat it as the same person.
assessment.maturity: Protocols are well established and experimentally realised over fibre and satellite links, but practical security remains limited by implementation loopholes, and the area has just been touched by the 2022 prize for entanglement experiments.
uncertainties: Practical security under real devices is not fully settled.
Wiesner's earlier conjugate-coding idea is not in the credited names.
